_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have shown for the first time that human heart muscle cells can regrow after a heart attack. The finding overturns the idea that damaged areas of the heart are completely incapable of regeneration. Scientists now hope to identify ways to dramatically boost this natural repair process, potentially opening a new path toward treatments for heart failure.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists capture two DNA strands zipping together for the first time
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] America’s Response Monument in New York, New York
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

This is a statue memorializing the U.S. Army’s Green Berets and other Special Forces soldiers who gallantly brought the fight to the Taliban in Afghanistan in the early days after September 11th.

During their action they spent time riding into combat on horseback along side their Afghan allies.  

The statue, by artist Douwe Blumberg, is 1 1/2 times life size and is a detailed version of a combat ready soldier on horseback.

Incorporated in the base of the statue is a piece of steel from the World Trade Center.

Liberty Park is elevated above the street level just to the south of the September 11th Memorial and Museum.

items.title: [Fast Company] Frozen blueberry recall expands to product sold at Walmart as E. coli hospitalizations rise
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Another blueberry product is being recalled due to concerns that it may be contaminated with E. coli.

The latest product is believed to be linked to an ongoing outbreak that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has been investigating since May. This time, the product was available at Walmart. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Back in May, the CDC began investigating a multi-state outbreak of E. coli infections. The outbreak was believed to be linked to blueberries.

In early July, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notified the public about a food recall associated with the outbreak.

As Fast Company reported at the time, that recalled product was Frozen GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries. It was manufactured by Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of San Carlos, Chile, and sold at Publix stores.

Then, in late July, the FDA again notified the public of another blueberry product recall, this one also related to the ongoing E. coli outbreak.

This second recall encompassed four additional GreenWise Organic products containing whole blueberries and whole mixed berries.

Now, yet another product is believed to be linked to the E. coli outbreak, which has expanded to include 17 infections, six of which have required hospitalization.

What additional product is being recalled?

On September 2, Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. announced a voluntary expansion of its previous recall. The FDA notified the public the next day.

That recall includes a single additional product:

  • Product: Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend 10 OZ (Including Strawberries, Blackberries and Blueberries), with UPC: 7874211226
  • Package Size: 10 oz
  • Lot Code: 6040 01-6 (in front of the package)
  • Best If Used By Date: February 9, 2028

Where was the recalled product sold?

The recalled Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend was sold at select Walmart stores in more than a dozen states, according to the recall notice. Those states include:

  • Alabama
  • Arkansas
  • Florida
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Kentucky
  • Louisiana
  • Minnesota
  • Mississippi
  • Missouri
  • North Carolina
  • Ohio
  • Oklahoma
  • South Carolina
  • Texas
  • Wisconsin

What should I do if I have the recalled products?

If you have the recalled product in your possession, you should not consume it. Instead, the recall notice instructs the consumer to dispose of the product or take it back to Walmart for a full refund.

How widespread is the blueberry E. coli outbreak?

According to a September 3 update from the CDC, the outbreak has so far resulted in 17 cases. Six of those individuals have required hospitalization. That’s a hospitalization rate of 35%.

So far, infections related to the outbreak are known to have occurred only in two states: Florida (13 cases) and Georgia (4 cases).

However, the FDA notes that while those infected are so far only from Georgia and Florida, the recalled products believed to be linked to the outbreak were distributed much more widely.

According to the FDA, the recalled products were distributed to the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Arkansas
  • Florida
  • Georgia
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Kentucky
  • Louisiana
  • Minnesota
  • Missouri
  • North Carolina
  • Ohio
  • Oklahoma
  • South Carolina
  • Tennessee
  • Texas
  • Virginia
  • Wisconsin

The CDC says the outbreak investigation is ongoing.

items.title: [Fast Company] 25 years after 9/11, some parts of air travel are starting to look familiar again. Here’s how much flying has changed
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

It’s hard to believe that 9/11 was 25 years ago today. On that day, September 11, 2001, I was a young journalist working at CNN headquarters, producing the noon newscast, when I saw the first, and then the second, plane crash into the World Trade Center in real time on the newsroom monitor.

In an instant, everything about air travel in America changed. And 9/11 has informed the way we have traveled ever since. Gone are the days when anybody could say goodbye to loved ones at the gate. (Although that restriction has recently begun to ease; more on that below.) Also gone, for the most part: the ability to run late and still make your flight in under half an hour.

Here are a few examples of what is different between then and now.

TSA airport security checks

While there were security checks before September 11, 2001, they were nothing in comparison to the invasive TSA screening checkpoints we have today. Those screenings are a direct result of the formation of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), which was created in November 2001, two months after the terrorist attacks.

Back then, there were no required Real IDs, no full-body screenings or mandatory metal detectors with enhanced screening technology, no need to show your ID before security, and certainly no invasive privacy measures such as facial scans employing facial recognition software.

Beyond just taking off our shoes or having to scan the contents of our carry-ons, those of us who remember long for the days when we could show up late to the gate, drink in hand, and board with relative ease.

Originally, the TSA was housed under the Department of Transportation (DOT), whose focus under the Aviation and Transportation Security Act (signed by then-President George Bush two months after the attacks) was to perform uniform, restrictive screening, and institute a federal takeover of airport security from private companies.

But in 2003, the agency moved to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Starting in 2011 with the launch of TSA PreCheck, TSA created a system that critics now argue over-screens the general public, treating every passenger as a threat instead of focusing on high-risk individuals. From body scans that employ advanced imaging technologies to restricting liquids, aerosols, and gels, airport security measures have made traveling a long, exhausting process. TSA screened 900 million people at airports in just 2025 alone.

In fact, today’s TSA’s Secure Flight program’s security measures “begin long before you arrive at the airport.” Most travelers are probably unaware that TSA screens passenger information, cross-listing it with intelligence and federal government watch lists—for both travel outside the U.S. but also within—before you even hit security.

Boarding passes

A boarding pass is now required to get to the gate. It wasn’t always. After the September 11 attacks, printed boarding passes became mandatory requirements to pass through security. By 2010, mobile boarding passes accessible from smartphones became standard.

However, this post-9/11 restriction is now starting to ease. In a welcome change for many, TSA is instituting TSA Gateside, which will ease restrictions on those who want to see off friends and family at the gate. As Fast Company previously reported, PreCheck members at select airports can now go to the gates to meet flights, even if they aren’t flying themselves.

Longer lines, even at TSA PreCheck

Since 9/11, airport wait times have occasionally averaged one to three hours at certain hubs, per NPR.

And according to a 2025 New York Times article, TSA PreCheck, which was created to cut down on the long lines formed by post-9/11 security checkpoints, doesn’t actually speed up travel by much. Reporters looked into travel at New York airports, and found PreCheck at John F. Kennedy, LaGuardia, and Newark airports only saved travelers about five to 10 minutes on average.

What travel restrictions have eased since 9/11?

Passengers have welcomed the end of the shoe removal rule, which, while not a direct result of 9/11, was also instituted around the same time.

Also expediting the security process: Some busy mothers now can access new dedicated lanes for families, as can veterans, at select airports.

items.title: [Fast Company] AI isn’t replacing jobs; it’s restructuring work
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Companies are racing to automate work without realizing they may also be automating away the systems that create expertise. That is the workforce challenge emerging beneath today’s AI conversation.

Most debates focus on whether AI will replace jobs. But jobs are the wrong lens for this discussion.

Work has always been made up of tasks, decisions, workflows, and capabilities bundled together under a title and scope. What AI is doing quite efficiently is unbundling that structure and redistributing the work itself. That changes how organizations create value. And it fundamentally changes how leaders should think about workforce strategy.

AI reshapes career ladders

ADP Research has been studying how AI is reshaping work in collaboration with researchers at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. One of the clearest signals emerging is that the impact of AI is not evenly distributed across organizations. While experienced workers may have anticipated disruption, in practice, many organizations are seeing something more nuanced.

AI performs exceptionally well against structured, repeatable, and rules-based work. Historically, that has often been the work assigned to junior employees. It is where people learn to build repetitions, pattern recognition, and operational judgment.

More experienced professionals tend to operate in environments where context, interpretation, and synthesis matter more. AI can accelerate that work, but it does not fully replace it. In many cases, expertise becomes more valuable in an AI-enabled environment because experienced workers know how to direct, evaluate, and refine machine output.

Experience becomes a multiplier, and that creates a more complicated workforce challenge than many organizations realize.

Erosion at the bottom

The real risk may not be displacement at the top of the organization, but erosion at the bottom.

Business leaders are already beginning to recognize the scale of this challenge as companies invest in upskilling workers to meet the changing nature of job roles and responsibilities. Yet upskilling alone doesn’t answer a more fundamental question: if AI increasingly performs the work where those capabilities were historically developed, how do organizations create the next generation of expertise?

Entry-level work has always served two functions simultaneously: generating operational output and developing future expertise. But as AI assumes more of the repetitive work that once served as a training ground, organizations need new ways to develop the judgment, pattern recognition, and decision-making capabilities that experience has historically created.

When organizations automate too much of that foundational layer too quickly, they risk weakening the long-term capability pipeline enterprises depend on. The challenge is no longer simply workforce automation; it is workforce architecture.

These questions will define the next generation of workforce strategy:

  • How do organizations develop judgment when traditional learning pathways disappear?
  • How do companies build expertise when repetitive work—historically the training ground for future leaders—is increasingly handled by machines?
  • How do enterprises redesign work without unintentionally constraining future talent development?

Answering these questions—not simply deploying AI faster—will separate organizations that build durable talent pipelines from those that quietly hollow them out.

From roles to capabilities

The implications extend well beyond hiring. As work becomes increasingly task-oriented and capability-based, traditional job descriptions become less meaningful than the capabilities individuals can apply across different contexts. Organizations are beginning to shift from static role structures toward capability systems built around a clear-eyed view of what skills exist inside the enterprise, which capabilities are increasing in value, and which activities should remain human-led. The work also requires understanding where AI enhances productivity versus where it introduces risk, and how human and machine work should be orchestrated together.

That transition affects nearly every workforce system: talent development, workforce planning, mobility, compensation, performance evaluation, organizational design, and leadership development. The future of workforce strategy is becoming less about managing roles and more about designing capability ecosystems.

Data as strategic visibility

Historically, payroll and workforce systems were viewed primarily through an administrative lens. But workforce data increasingly provides visibility into how work is performed across organizations: where expertise is concentrated, how workflows operate, where friction exists, and how value moves through the enterprise.

For organizations navigating AI transformation, that visibility becomes strategic.

Companies that understand how work flows through their organizations will redesign faster and more intelligently than those relying on static org charts and outdated role structures.

At the same time, enterprise leaders must recognize that AI adoption inside workforce systems operates differently than consumer AI experimentation.

HR, payroll, benefits, workforce compliance, and employee systems are deeply interconnected, compliance-driven environments. Accountability cannot disappear simply because software becomes more capable.

This is why the future of enterprise AI will not simply be defined by automation. It will be defined by orchestration: where human oversight remains necessary, how accountability is maintained, how workflows are redesigned responsibly, and how organizations preserve trust while increasing efficiency.

While consumer AI optimizes convenience, enterprise AI must optimize accountability. That distinction will shape the next generation of workforce systems.

Redesign work intentionally

Companies succeeding with AI are not treating it purely as a productivity tool. They are redesigning work intentionally. They are using AI to remove friction while elevating human contribution toward high-value activities: interpretation, relationship management, creativity, judgment, and strategic decision-making.

The future of work is not humans versus AI. It is about understanding which systems, decisions, and capabilities are best handled by machines and which remain fundamentally human. The organizations that approach this transition thoughtfully will create stronger, more adaptive workforce models.

The organizations that pursue automation without redesign risk weakening the very capabilities they will depend on most in the future. As leaders rethink work for the AI era, the most important question may no longer be, “What can AI automate?” but “How do we continue developing the human capabilities that organizations will depend on most?” The companies that answer that question well won’t just adopt AI more successfully—they have the potential to build stronger, more resilient organizations for the long term.

Usman “Oz” Khan is senior vice president of ADP Ventures.
